title: Seattle Is Obsessed With Dosa: Google Maps Shows 136% Jump in Mentions
excerpt: Google Maps' first Fan-Favourite Dining List finds reviews mentioning the South Indian staple up 136% year-on-year across the Emerald City.
body:
• Google Maps' first Fan-Favourite Dining List reports a 136% year-on-year rise in Seattle reviews mentioning dosas — one of the biggest single-dish surges on the list.
  • The list, built from reviews, ratings and aggregated direction requests across 10 world cities between September 2025 and August 2026, names Shri Ananda Bhavan and Chennai Express as Seattle's dosa hotspots.
  • Other findings: frozen yoghurt is back in New York (up 320%), mochi is surging in Tokyo (up 168%), and matcha keeps climbing across nearly all 10 cities.
  • Planning a Seattle trip? The full interactive list is live at mapsfanfavorites.withgoogle.com — search the Seattle tab for dosa spots near you.

In India, the dosa hardly needs an introduction: the crisp, fermented rice-and-lentil crepe is a breakfast staple and a comfort order at every South Indian restaurant. What it apparently needed was an introduction to Seattle — and judging by new Google Maps data, the two have now met. Reviews mentioning “dosas” in the US city rose 136% year-on-year, making the humble South Indian dish one of the standout food trends in Google's first-ever Fan-Favourite Dining List.

The list, announced this week, is Google's first dining guide built on real-world behaviour: reviews, ratings and aggregated requests for directions, gathered across 10 cities deemed global hot spots — Atlanta, Chicago, London, Melbourne, Montreal, New York, San Francisco, Santiago, Seattle and Tokyo. A live hub at mapsfanfavorites.withgoogle.com lets users browse each city by essentials, occasions and items trending in reviews.

What the numbers show

The 2026 list draws on Google Maps data from September 2025 through August 2026, including reviews and ratings from the Local Guides community, aggregated searches for directions and a final verification pass. Dosa's 136% jump in Seattle sits among the sharpest single-item surges in the report: for comparison, frozen yoghurt mentions rose 320% in New York, mochi mentions 168% in Tokyo, cinnamon buns 84% in Montreal, hojicha 114% in London and ube 75% in Melbourne. Matcha kept climbing in nearly every city, with Chicago up 82% and Santiago 84%.

“Our first-ever Fan-Favorite list spotlights top local restaurants and culinary trends across 10 cities — made possible only by Google Maps and the billions of people who use it to find, review, and rate places to eat.”

— Andrew Duchi, director of product management at Google

In Seattle, the report points dosa hunters toward Shri Ananda Bhavan and Chennai Express — two names familiar to anyone who has asked a South Indian in the Emerald City where to eat. The data does not say exactly what is driving the surge, but the likeliest explanation is the simplest: more people tried it, more people wrote about it, and the city's growing appetite did the rest.

Why dosa, why Seattle

Seattle is, in many ways, an obvious place for this to happen. The city's tech corridor — home to large Amazon and Microsoft workforces — has one of the densest South Indian diaspora populations in the United States, and its Indian restaurant scene has quietly deepened over the past decade. What was once a landscape of generic curry houses now includes dedicated South Indian kitchens, Kerala specialists and dosa-focused counters, giving newcomers and the merely curious plenty of on-ramps.

The dosa itself helps. Naturally gluten-free, customisable, and vegetarian-friendly, it fits neatly into the dietary Venn diagram of the Pacific Northwest — and its theatre, the dramatic spread of batter on a screaming-hot griddle, makes it one of the most photogenic dishes in Indian cuisine. In a ranking built partly on what people photograph, review and rave about, that matters.

The diaspora angle

For Indian-Americans, there is something quietly satisfying about watching a dish their grandmothers made on Sunday mornings show up in a Google trend report alongside froyo and beignets. Indian food's American journey — from the butter-chicken era of the 1990s to today's regional specificity — has been driven in large part by the diaspora itself: the restaurants families opened, the lunchboxes colleagues got curious about, the second-generation food writers who insisted there was more to the cuisine than the greatest-hits menu.

A 136% jump in review mentions is, strictly speaking, a measure of chatter rather than consumption. But chatter is how food trends start, and for a dish that spent decades as an insider order, being Seattle's most talked-about bite is a milestone worth noting. Pass the sambar.
